games.explanation: Wheeler is the best pitcher in this game and it isn't especially close, which is exactly why a plus-money dog against him is more interesting than the board treats it. The Orioles don't need to solve him, they need to survive him for five innings and let a hitters' park with the wind blowing out do the rest against a Phillies bullpen that has been leaking runs. Bradish has quietly been striking out more than a third of the hitters he's faced, and this is the kind of muggy, homer-friendly night where a Schwarber swing is the only real threat behind him. Baltimore's lineup is stacked with lefties who chase less than most of Wheeler's usual victims, and that's the sneaky part the market keeps ignoring. At +120 on the better roster in the friendlier park, you're getting paid to bet the wrong favorite.

Cade Cavalli's split lines tell a story the market apparently didn't read: he has been a completely different pitcher against right-handed bats, and Atlanta happens to run out a lineup full of them. Acuña, Olson, and Baldwin are exactly the profile that has been tattooing him, with righties posting a .458 wOBA against Cavalli while lefties barely scratch .300. Pair that with the better team by a wide margin on the Elo side, and -116 for a team the model makes closer to a 65 percent favorite is the kind of gap you take without thinking too hard. Washington's offense is thin behind Wood, and thin offenses don't scare a lineup this deep.

Liberatore is the kind of lefty who survives on the platoon split and gets exposed the second a right-handed lineup takes a good look at him, and Toronto happens to trot out one of the more punishing right-handed cores in the league. Guerrero and Springer against this arm profile is the entire pitch, with Vlad in particular sporting a .455 xwOBA versus lefties that turns Liberatore's contact problems into a real issue. Scherzer isn't the Scherzer of 2018 but he doesn't need to be against a Cardinals lineup where Walker is striking out in a third of his trips and the supporting cast is thin. The market has this closer to a coin flip when the better team, the better rotation slot, and the better matchup all sit on the same side. -114 on the favorite that should be juicier is the whole reason we're here.

Gavin Williams is a strikeout arm who forgets where the plate is often enough that a patient lineup can just sit and wait for the free base. Arizona happens to be that lineup, with Perdomo barely striking out and a Marte-Carroll core that punishes any righty who nibbles. Williams is walking better than eleven percent of hitters he faces this year, and Merrill Kelly is quietly the steadier starter in this game by every expected-contact metric that matters. Getting a dog price on the better team, the better rotation arm, and the more disciplined lineup is the entire thesis, and +144 is generous for it.

The market is treating this like a road dog getting a favor, but the Cubs are the better team on paper and the plus price is doing all the work for us. Colin Rea isn't going to overpower anyone, yet the Yankees are trotting out a lineup where the middle bats punish lefties more than righties, which is exactly the wrong side of the platoon to be on tonight. Meanwhile Michael Busch is quietly running a .400 wOBA against right-handers and Suzuki keeps barreling everything in sight, so Chicago's top four is a real problem. Wrigley plays down, the projected score is a genuine coin flip, and the price says otherwise. At +112 on the better club, take the math.

The market is looking at a pick-em because Detroit is trotting out Keider Montero, and completely ignoring that the team behind him is several classes above the Athletics in every column that matters. Tigers-A's should not be a coin flip, and pricing it like one is how you give the sharper side a free roll on the better roster. Detroit's Elo edge here is roughly 190 points, the kind of gap you almost never see laid at even money, and the lineup gets to feast on an Oakland staff that keeps handing out hard contact. Jacob Wilson's shiny wOBA hides an xwOBA that tells you the regression is coming, and it doesn't have to arrive tonight for this ticket to cash. Getting the better team at a plus-ish number is the entire pitch.

Kirby's ERA still reads like an ace, but the underlying contact profile has been quietly leaking all year, and Minnesota happens to bring the exact lineup built to punish it. Josh Bell has been mashing right-handed pitching to the tune of a .384 xwOBA, and Kody Clemens and Larnach round out a middle that hits the ball hard whether the results have shown up yet or not. Bradley is the shakier arm on paper, but a closed roof in a pitcher's park caps the downside on both sides, and the sim lands on a one-run game the market is pricing like a coin flip tilted the wrong way. Getting the better Elo team at plus money in a projected 3-run environment is the whole ballgame.

The market is treating this like a Dodgers home game against a soft opponent, when it's actually a coin flip being sold at plus money. Boston is the higher-rated team by a comfortable margin, and Sheehan's shiny surface line hides a walk problem that gets uglier the deeper you dig, particularly against left-handed bats he's issued free passes to at a 12.7% clip. Contreras and Abreu are exactly the kind of hard-contact righty-and-lefty combo that punishes command wobble, and the sim has this game landing inside a run either way. Getting +142 on the better roster in a projected one-run fight is the entire argument.
